title: Trump DOJ Weaponized Against Political Opponents Including Comey, James, Cuomo
description_short: Trump DOJ Weaponized Against Political Opponents Including Comey, James, Cuomo
description_medium: By September 2025, the Justice Department had opened or advanced investigations involving several of Donald Trump’s political adversaries, including James Comey, Letitia James, Andrew Cuomo, John Bolton, and LaMonica McIver. Trump publicly urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to move faster on prosecutions. The pattern drew criticism from former prosecutors and legal scholars, who described the department as using criminal enforcement against perceived opponents.
description_long: By September 2025, Trump's Justice Department had opened or escalated criminal investigations against a sweeping list of political opponents including former FBI Director James Comey (indicted September 26, 2025 for allegedly lying to Congress), New York Attorney General Letitia James (grand jury convened investigating her civil fraud cases against Trump and the NRA), former Governor Andrew Cuomo, former national security adviser John Bolton, and Representative LaMonica McIver (D-NJ). Trump publicly pressured Attorney General Pam Bondi via social media to accelerate prosecutions. Georgetown law professor Paul Butler described the department as simultaneously deprioritizing fighting public corruption while weaponizing the DOJ against people Trump doesn't like. Former prosecutors noted Trump's former personal attorneys now occupied key positions and had fired dozens of career prosecutors. A September 2025 AP analysis found the DOJ had also classified liberal activist groups as potential domestic terrorist organizations. Legal experts described the pattern as unprecedented since Nixon.

title: Nunes Memo: Republicans Distort FISA Surveillance to Attack Russia Probe
description_short: Nunes Memo: Republicans Distort FISA Surveillance to Attack Russia Probe
description_medium: On February 2, 2018, House Republicans released a memo alleging that the FBI and Justice Department misused FISA surveillance to investigate Trump campaign aide Carter Page. The FBI said the memo was misleading and incomplete; Democrats issued a counter-memo describing omitted context about the surveillance applications. Trump called the release total vindication, though it did not end the Russia investigation.
description_long: On February 2, 2018, Republicans on the House Intelligence Committee under Chairman Devin Nunes released a declassified four-page memo claiming that FBI and DOJ officials abused the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act to obtain a wiretap warrant on Trump campaign aide Carter Page using the Steele dossier. The memo, which FBI Director Christopher Wray and DOJ officials strongly disputed as misleading and incomplete, was framed by Trump as proving 'total vindication' in the Russia investigation. Democrats released a counter-memo demonstrating that the Nunes memo omitted critical facts, including that the Page surveillance was based on multiple sources and that the FBI had already been investigating Page before the dossier. The episode was widely seen as a politically coordinated attack on the FBI and the integrity of the Russia investigation. Multiple Republican members of the committee later acknowledged they had not reviewed the underlying classified material before voting to release the memo.

title: Trump Media DJT Stock: Meme Stock Manipulation Concerns
description_short: Trump Media DJT Stock: Meme Stock Manipulation Concerns
description_medium: Trump Media & Technology Group began trading under ticker DJT after its 2024 SPAC merger, with Donald Trump holding a majority stake. CEO Devin Nunes accused several trading firms of manipulating the stock, while market data showed it on Nasdaq’s threshold-security list. A later short position led the company to ask the SEC to investigate; the agency did not publicly comment on that request.
description_long: Trump Media & Technology Group (ticker: DJT) went public via SPAC merger on March 26, 2024, with Trump owning approximately 53% of the company. From April 2024 onward, DJT appeared continuously on Nasdaq's Regulation SHO Threshold Security List — a designation indicating potential illegal naked short-selling — for over two months straight. Trump Media CEO Devin Nunes filed letters to Congress and Nasdaq claiming market manipulation, naming Citadel Securities, VIRTU Americas, G1 Execution Services, and Jane Street Capital as responsible for over 60% of extraordinary trading volume. By April 2025, hedge fund Qube Research disclosed a $105 million short position, prompting Trump Media to ask Trump's own SEC to investigate the shorts — a request the agency declined to comment on. Critics noted the irony of a president using a captured regulator to defend his personal stock position while that same regulator dropped dozens of crypto cases benefiting his other ventures.

title: Kushner Affinity Partners Grows to $4.8B as Gulf Sovereign Funds Pour In During Trump Presidency
description_short: Kushner Affinity Partners Grows to $4.8B as Gulf Sovereign Funds Pour In During Trump Presidency
description_medium: Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners reported $4.8 billion in assets by March 2025 after new commitments from Abu Dhabi and Qatar. The growth followed a $2 billion Saudi investment in 2021, despite concerns raised by the fund’s screening panel about Kushner’s experience and public profile. A Senate Finance Committee report said the firm had collected management fees without returning profits, prompting questions about conflicts and investor returns.
description_long: Jared Kushner's private equity firm Affinity Partners — founded six months after he left the White House — grew to $4.8 billion in assets under management by March 2025, up from $3 billion the prior year, driven by new $1.5 billion commitments from Abu Dhabi-based Lunate and the Qatar Investment Authority. The Saudi Public Investment Fund had originally invested $2 billion in 2021 despite its own screening panel citing Kushner's 'inexperience,' 'unsatisfactory' due diligence results, and 'public relations risks' from his White House role; the PIF board overruled the panel. As of a September 2024 Senate Finance Committee report, Affinity had collected at least $112 million in management fees while returning zero profits to investors — prompting Senator Ron Wyden to question whether the fund was structured primarily to pay the Kushner family rather than generate returns. The expansion of Gulf investment accelerated in direct proportion to Trump's return to power.

title: Melania's Unauthorized Modeling and the 'Einstein Visa' She Received Anyway
description_short: Melania's Unauthorized Modeling and the 'Einstein Visa' She Received Anyway
description_medium: An Associated Press investigation reported that Melania Trump received $20,056 for ten U.S. modeling assignments before her H-1B work visa began in October 1996. She had entered on a visitor visa that did not authorize paid work. Later reporting examined her EB-1 “extraordinary ability” green-card status. The disclosures drew attention because Donald Trump was campaigning on strict immigration enforcement.
description_long: An Associated Press investigation published November 5, 2016 revealed that Melania Trump was paid $20,056 for 10 modeling assignments in the United States between September 10 and October 15, 1996, during the seven weeks before she received her H-1B work visa on October 18, 1996. She had entered the country on a B-1/B-2 visitor visa, under which paid employment is prohibited. The disclosure was particularly pointed because her husband had built his campaign on strict immigration enforcement and E-verify proposals. Subsequently, reporting revealed that Melania received an EB-1 Einstein visa for persons of extraordinary ability to obtain her green card in 2001, at a time when her American modeling portfolio consisted primarily of a Camel cigarette billboard and a Sports Illustrated swimsuit appearance — credentials that immigration lawyers and lawmakers debated fiercely as failing to meet the extraordinary-ability standard that Nobel laureates and Olympic athletes use the same pathway to satisfy.

title: DOGE Deploys Musk Grok AI on Sensitive Federal Government Data
description_short: DOGE Deploys Musk Grok AI on Sensitive Federal Government Data
description_medium: Reuters reported that DOGE teams were using a customized version of Elon Musk’s Grok AI to analyze sensitive federal data at Homeland Security by May 2025, potentially at other agencies as well. The report cited three sources and said the deployment lacked normal agency approval. Experts raised conflict-of-interest and privacy concerns because Musk owned xAI while leading DOGE and could benefit from government use of its product.
description_long: By May 2025, DOGE teams were using a customized version of Elon Musk's Grok artificial intelligence chatbot — built by his company xAI — to analyze sensitive federal government data at the Department of Homeland Security and potentially other agencies, according to Reuters reporting based on three sources. The deployment occurred without proper agency approval and raised potential violations of conflict-of-interest laws, as Musk stood to benefit commercially from his AI product gaining government contracts and exposure to federal datasets. DOGE had by this point accumulated access to data across at least seven major departments. Experts warned that using Musk's proprietary commercial AI on government data gave xAI a potential competitive advantage over rivals and exposed sensitive personal information on millions of Americans to a privately-held company owned by the head of DOGE itself — a person simultaneously running Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI while serving as a de facto senior government official.

title: Measles Epidemic: 700+ Cases, 3 Deaths, RFK Blames Everything but Vaccines
description_short: Measles Epidemic: 700+ Cases, 3 Deaths, RFK Blames Everything but Vaccines
description_medium: A measles outbreak that began in West Texas spread to neighboring states and exceeded 700 confirmed U.S. cases by April 2025. Three people died, including two children in Texas. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. promoted treatments such as vitamin A and described vaccination as a personal choice rather than making a clear public call to vaccinate. Scientists warned that measles could again spread widely.
description_long: In early 2025, a measles outbreak began in a tight-knit religious community in West Texas and spread across New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Kansas — ultimately becoming one of the worst U.S. outbreaks in 25 years with over 700 confirmed cases by April 2025. Three people died: two children in Texas and an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico, marking the first measles deaths in the U.S. since 2015. HHS Secretary RFK Jr. responded not with a unified call to vaccinate, but by promoting unproven treatments including vitamin A, steroids, and cod liver oil, writing in a Fox News op-ed that 'the decision to vaccinate is a personal one.' Scientists warned the U.S. was at a tipping point for the return of endemic measles — declared eradicated nationally in 2000. Kennedy also revived debunked claims in May 2025 that the measles vaccine contains 'fetal debris,' contradicting decades of evidence that the MMR vaccine is safe.

title: Trump Paid $750 in Federal Income Tax Both 2016 and 2017 — NYT Investigation
description_short: Trump Paid $750 in Federal Income Tax Both 2016 and 2017 — NYT Investigation
description_medium: A 2020 New York Times investigation of Donald Trump’s tax records reported that he paid $750 in federal income taxes in both 2016 and 2017, and none in ten of the prior fifteen years. The reporting attributed the low amounts largely to business losses. It also described an IRS audit of a large refund claim whose outcome could have led to substantial repayment.
description_long: The New York Times's landmark September 27, 2020 investigation into two decades of Donald Trump's tax records revealed that Trump had paid only $750 in federal income taxes in 2016, the year he was elected president, and $750 in 2017, his first year in office. In 10 of the preceding 15 years, Trump had paid no federal income taxes at all, primarily by reporting business losses that offset income. The findings directly contradicted Trump's public image as a massively successful billionaire. Trump had paid a combined $5.2 million in federal taxes in 2018 and 2019 that were largely covered by tax refunds he had claimed. The IRS was conducting an audit of a $72.9 million refund Trump had claimed, the outcome of which could require him to repay $100 million in taxes plus penalties and interest. The investigation was a landmark work of investigative journalism that reshaped public understanding of Trump's financial reality.

title: Alien Enemies Act Invoked Against Venezuelan Nationals, March 2025
description_short: Alien Enemies Act Invoked Against Venezuelan Nationals, March 2025
description_medium: On March 14, 2025, President Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act against Venezuelan nationals identified as members of Tren de Aragua, seeking deportations without ordinary immigration proceedings. A federal judge issued an order halting removals, but the administration completed some deportation flights while disputing when the written order took effect. The episode triggered litigation over executive authority, due process, and compliance with court orders.
description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed Proclamation 10903 invoking the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — last used by FDR during WWII — to declare Tren de Aragua (TdA) a hostile invading force and subject all Venezuelan nationals aged 14 or older who are TdA members to immediate summary deportation without standard immigration proceedings. The State Department had designated TdA a Foreign Terrorist Organization on February 20, 2025. Within hours of the proclamation, the ACLU filed suit and Chief Judge James Boasberg of the D.C. District Court issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportations, verbally ordering flights already in the air to turn around. The administration defied his verbal order, completing deportations anyway; the DOJ argued the written order had not yet been issued when the planes departed. Legal scholars widely criticized the proclamation's framing of immigration as a wartime 'invasion' as a radical distortion of a law written for actual declared wars.

title: Day 1: Border Emergency Declared, Birthright Citizenship Ended by EO
description_short: Day 1: Border Emergency Declared, Birthright Citizenship Ended by EO
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump declared a border emergency and signed an order purporting to end birthright citizenship for some U.S.-born children. The order directed agencies to withhold citizenship documentation in specified cases and was quickly blocked by federal courts. Trump also shut down the CBP One appointment system, canceling more than 270,000 scheduled legal entry appointments and leaving migrants waiting in Mexico.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, within hours of taking office, President Trump signed a national emergency declaration at the southern border and issued an executive order purporting to end birthright citizenship — a right enshrined in the 14th Amendment since 1868. The birthright citizenship order instructed federal agencies to stop issuing documentation recognizing U.S. citizenship to children born to mothers unlawfully present in the United States if the father was not a citizen or lawful permanent resident. Trump simultaneously shut down the CBP One app, canceling over 270,000 existing legal entry appointments with no notice, stranding migrants in dangerous border regions of Mexico. Federal courts immediately blocked the birthright citizenship order as unconstitutional, with one district judge calling it 'blatantly unconstitutional' before a Supreme Court case ensued over nationwide injunctions. The barrage of Day 1 immigration EOs — totaling roughly 10 actions — represented the largest single-day executive restructuring of U.S. immigration law in modern history.

title: Rumeysa Ozturk: Tufts PhD Student Arrested for Pro-Palestine Op-Ed
description_short: Rumeysa Ozturk: Tufts PhD Student Arrested for Pro-Palestine Op-Ed
description_medium: DHS agents arrested Tufts doctoral student Rumeysa Ozturk on March 25, 2025, after she co-authored a campus newspaper op-ed criticizing the university’s response to calls for divestment. The administration alleged support for Hamas, while the cited op-ed was the stated basis for the action. She was transferred to Louisiana and detained for more than six weeks before a judge ordered her release, citing the chilling effect on speech.
description_long: On March 25, 2025, DHS agents in plainclothes arrested Rumeysa Ozturk, 30, a Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University with a valid F-1 visa, as she left her Somerville, Massachusetts apartment to break her Ramadan fast with friends. Video of her screaming as she was grabbed went viral. The administration alleged she 'engaged in activities in support of Hamas' — the sole basis was a 2024 op-ed she co-wrote in the Tufts student newspaper criticizing the university's response to calls to divest from Israeli-linked companies. DHS moved her to an ICE detention facility in Louisiana despite a judge's order not to transfer her out of state without notice. After over six weeks of detention, U.S. District Judge William Sessions ordered her immediate release on May 9, 2025, ruling that her continued detention 'chills free speech' of non-citizens. Secretary of State Rubio acknowledged revoking more than 300 student visas and said he was revoking more daily.

title: Family Separation 2.0: 600 Children in Federal Shelters, Highest Since Records Began
description_short: Family Separation 2.0: 600 Children in Federal Shelters, Highest Since Records Began
description_medium: ProPublica reported that ICE placements of immigrant children in federal shelters reached about 600 from January 2025, the highest level in a decade of records. Many cases followed parents’ arrests inside the United States during traffic stops, workplace raids, or courthouse appearances. The reporting also described longer shelter stays and families separated from U.S.-citizen children, drawing comparisons with the first Trump administration’s separation policy.
description_long: Since January 2025, ICE placed approximately 600 immigrant children into federal shelters — more than the previous four years combined, and the highest number since recordkeeping began a decade earlier, according to ProPublica data published November 2025. Unlike the 2018 'zero-tolerance' border separations, the second-term separations occurred inside the United States after ICE arrested parents during traffic stops (in approximately 150 documented cases), workplace raids, and courthouse arrests, with children left behind or transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement. Of the 320,000 ICE detention book-ins in FY2026, nearly 17,900 were of people who self-reported as parents of U.S.-citizen children — nearly double FY2024. A New York Times report from August 2025 documented a Russian family separated at JFK Airport where their 8-year-old son Maksim was sent to an unaccompanied minors shelter; the last contact was May 15, 2025. The average shelter stay for children grew to nearly six months, up from one month under Biden.

title: Trump Fires All Three Election Assistance Commission Members Before Midterms
description_short: Trump Fires All Three Election Assistance Commission Members Before Midterms
description_medium: On July 9, 2026, President Trump removed the three remaining members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission less than four months before the midterm elections. The agency supports election administration, certifies voting systems, and distributes security grants. One Republican commissioner had resigned earlier, while another was reportedly pressured to leave. The firings left the commission without members and raised concerns about election oversight and executive control.
description_long: On July 9, 2026 — less than four months before the November midterms — President Trump fired all three remaining members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, leaving the federal agency that certifies voting systems, distributes election security grants, and maintains the national voter registration form without any commissioners. Democratic commissioners Thomas Hicks and Benjamin W. Hovland received brief termination emails from White House aide Morgan DeWitt Snow. Republican commissioner Christy McCormick was pressured to resign. A fourth commissioner, Republican Don Palmer, had already resigned in April for a Heritage Foundation post. The White House justified the firings by citing the Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling expanding presidential authority to remove independent agency members. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it a brazen attempt to seize control of our elections before a single vote is cast. With CISA already gutted, the EAC was one of the few remaining federal entities providing election security support to states.

title: US Withdraws from 66 International Organizations in Mass Exit
description_short: US Withdraws from 66 International Organizations in Mass Exit
description_medium: On January 7, 2026, President Trump signed a memorandum withdrawing the United States from 66 international organizations, conventions, and treaties after a State Department review. The list included major climate bodies such as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. The White House said the organizations conflicted with U.S. interests and sovereignty; scholars questioned whether the president could withdraw unilaterally from treaty-based bodies.
description_long: On January 7, 2026, Trump signed an executive memorandum withdrawing the United States from 66 international organizations, conventions, and treaties following a review by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The mass withdrawal included the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change — the treaty underpinning all international climate agreements — and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the world's leading authority on climate science. Additional withdrawals covered the International Solar Alliance, the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance, the Global Counter-Terrorism Forum, the UN Register of Conventional Arms, and dozens of other multilateral bodies. Nearly half of the 66 entities were UN-affiliated. The White House stated the organizations no longer serve American interests and promote ineffective or hostile agendas, including radical climate policies, global governance and ideological programs that conflict with US sovereignty. Constitutional scholars noted that many of these were multilateral bodies established by Senate-ratified treaties, raising questions about whether Trump had unilateral authority to exit.

title: Trump Approves Federal Aid for Potomac Sewage Crisis After Escalating Political Clash
description_short: Trump Approves Federal Aid for Potomac Sewage Crisis After Escalating Political Clash
description_medium: After a January 19 pipeline rupture released at least 250 million gallons of sewage into the Potomac River, Washington, D.C., requested federal emergency help. FEMA said President Trump approved equipment and response resources after Mayor Muriel Bowser declared an emergency. Trump had criticized local Democratic leaders over the spill, making the aid decision part of a broader political dispute about responsibility and federal-state coordination.
description_long: President Donald Trump has approved emergency assistance to Washington, D.C., to help the city address a sewage system leak that dumped at least 250 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. The Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Trump’s approval on Saturday, allowing FEMA to provide equipment and resources to help with the response to the Jan. 19 spill after a pipeline ruptured. D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser had requested the federal help on Wednesday and declared an emergency. Trump’s approval of the disaster relief request comes after he criticized the handling of the spill, blaming local Democratic leaders and focusing especially on Maryland’s Democratic Gov. Wes Moore. Taken together, the episode showed how Trump's current governing style continues to centralize power, push legal limits, and shift institutional norms in ways that raise long-tail accountability risk. The event also intensified concerns about downstream harm to due process, regulatory integrity, or federal-state coordination depending on the policy domain involved.

title: National Guard Deployed to Chicago and Portland Over Democratic Governors Objections
description_short: National Guard Deployed to Chicago and Portland Over Democratic Governors Objections
description_medium: From September through November 2025, the Trump administration sent National Guard troops toward Chicago and Portland over objections from Illinois and Oregon officials, describing anti-ICE protests as insurrection. Courts temporarily blocked deployments, and Trump threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act. Governors J.B. Pritzker and Tina Kotek challenged the moves, arguing the deployments were political and lacked a lawful basis.
description_long: From September through November 2025, Trump dispatched National Guard troops to Chicago and Portland over the explicit objections of Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker and Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, framing anti-ICE protests in both cities as criminal insurrection. In October 2025, Trump threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act to sidestep court orders blocking the deployments. Hundreds of Texas National Guard soldiers gathered near Chicago while a federal judge had temporarily barred troops from Portland. Illinois Governor Pritzker accused Trump of using troops as a political tool and filed suit. NBC News reported in October 2025 that White House discussions had shifted from whether to invoke the Insurrection Act to how and when. Stephen Miller described the anti-ICE protests as an all-out campaign of insurrection against the sovereignty of the United States. The Supreme Court had not yet ruled on the legal boundaries. Legal experts warned that invoking the Insurrection Act against peaceful protesters would mark an unprecedented authoritarian escalation.

title: Supreme Court Orders Trump to Facilitate Return of Wrongly Deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia
description_short: Supreme Court Orders Trump to Facilitate Return of Wrongly Deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia
description_medium: On April 10, 2025, the Supreme Court directed the Trump administration to facilitate Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s return after he was mistakenly deported to El Salvador despite a court-ordered stay. The administration acknowledged the deportation was an error, and Garcia was held in a Salvadoran prison. The 8–1 order required the government to work toward his return while leaving implementation details to lower courts.
description_long: On April 10, 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court — in an 8-1 unsigned order — directed the Trump administration to 'facilitate' the return of Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who had been living in Maryland with his family and had a court-ordered stay of removal, who was nonetheless deported to El Salvador and sent to the brutal CECOT maximum-security prison in an acknowledged administrative error. The administration had admitted in court that Abrego Garcia's deportation was a mistake. The Supreme Court's rare and rapid intervention underscored the gravity of the situation — a man had been wrongly imprisoned in a foreign torture facility against explicit court orders. The unanimous nature of the order, joined even by justices appointed by Trump, signaled that the Court viewed the administration's conduct as an affront to basic constitutional principles. Legal scholars called the case a test of whether constitutional rights and court orders retained any meaning under the Trump administration.

title: Trump Deploys Marines and Federalized National Guard to Los Angeles Over Protests
description_short: Trump Deploys Marines and Federalized National Guard to Los Angeles Over Protests
description_medium: On June 7, 2025, Trump sent about 2,000 California National Guard troops and 700 Marines to Los Angeles during protests against ICE raids, overriding Governor Gavin Newsom’s control of the Guard. Newsom challenged the deployment, and federal courts disputed whether the statutory requirements were met and whether Marines could take part in domestic law enforcement. The Ninth Circuit later partially reversed one ruling.
description_long: On June 7, 2025, Trump issued a presidential memorandum deploying approximately 2,000 California National Guard troops — taken from Governor Gavin Newsom's control against his explicit objections — plus 700 active-duty Marines to Los Angeles in response to protests against ICE immigration raids. The administration labeled the protests a possible form of rebellion against the authority of the U.S. government. Newsom called the deployment unnecessary and counterproductive. Federal Judge Charles Breyer issued a temporary restraining order on June 12, ruling Trump had failed to meet the legal prerequisites under 10 U.S.C. 12406. A federal judge later ruled the Marines' presence violated the Posse Comitatus Act, which bars the military from domestic law enforcement. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals partially reversed. The administration deployed up to 4,000 National Guard personnel and relied on legal theories of implied presidential protective power for the Marines. Legal scholars described it as the most aggressive domestic military deployment against civilian protesters in decades.

title: The $60 Trump Bible: Holy Week Merchandise Grift Earns $1.3M in Royalties
description_short: The $60 Trump Bible: Holy Week Merchandise Grift Earns $1.3M in Royalties
description_medium: Donald Trump promoted the “God Bless the USA Bible,” a $59.99 edition combining scripture with U.S. founding documents and the Pledge of Allegiance. The product was announced during Holy Week in March 2024 and co-branded with singer Lee Greenwood. A later financial disclosure, reported by the Washington Post, listed about $1.3 million in royalties. The sale prompted criticism from religious leaders about commercializing religious imagery for political benefit.
description_long: On March 26, 2024 — during Holy Week and Lent — Trump announced the 'God Bless the USA Bible' co-branded with country singer Lee Greenwood, sold at $59.99 per copy, featuring the Constitution, Declaration of Independence, and Pledge of Allegiance alongside biblical text. Trump recorded a promotional video declaring 'I love the Bible. It’s my favorite book,' despite having famously failed to cite a single verse or chapter when repeatedly asked by interviewers over the years. The Washington Post reported Trump earned approximately $1.3 million in royalties from Bible sales, adding religious merchandise to a portfolio that already included NFTs, sneakers, and meme coins. The announcement drew immediate criticism from Christian leaders across the spectrum — including the Southern Baptist Convention’s Russell Moore — who called it 'a grotesque use of the sacred for profit.' The Bible grift represents Trump’s consistent strategy of harvesting evangelical loyalty as a commercial revenue stream while demonstrating no personal theological literacy or sincerity.

title: Iran Nuclear Talks Collapse After Five Rounds
description_short: Iran Nuclear Talks Collapse After Five Rounds
description_medium: The Trump administration held five rounds of nuclear talks with Iran from April to May 2025, mediated by Oman. Envoy Steve Witkoff shifted from discussing limited uranium enrichment to demanding that Iran dismantle enrichment entirely, while Iranian officials called enrichment non-negotiable. The fifth round ended without a conclusive agreement. The supplied account says Trump later issued ultimatums and ordered strikes without returning to negotiations.
description_long: From April through May 2025, the Trump administration conducted five rounds of nuclear negotiations with Iran — the first such direct US-Iran diplomatic contact since 2017 — mediated by Oman and held in Muscat and Rome. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff initially floated allowing Iran to enrich uranium at 3.67%, then reversed course demanding total dismantlement of all enrichment capability, which he called a red line. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called enrichment non-negotiable. By the fifth round in Rome on May 23, Oman's mediator reported some but not conclusive progress. Witkoff left early. Iran had accelerated enrichment to 60% purity, enough to produce material for over a dozen weapons within weeks. A bipartisan letter signed by 52 senators and 177 representatives warned Trump against any deal allowing Iran to retain any enrichment capability. Talks formally collapsed when Trump, frustrated with the pace, privately issued ultimatums to Tehran and then ordered military strikes without returning to negotiations, bypassing Congress entirely.
